laws_treaties: Republic Act No. 6426 (Foreign Currency Deposit Act)
Civil Code, Article 10 (right and justice to prevail)

stances.claim: The basic principle of statutory construction is to find the meaning intended by the framers and apply it to the facts -- via either verba legis or ratio legis, and 'the question seems simple but there is no simple answer.'
stances.rhetorical_move: frame-setting (acknowledging the simplicity of the question and the complexity of the answer)

stances.claim: Under verba legis (plain meaning), if a statute is clear, plain, and free from ambiguity, it must be accorded its literal meaning without other rules of interpretation -- interpretation is resorted to only when the literal meaning would be 'impossible, absurd or would lead to injustice.'
stances.rhetorical_move: rule-statement with exception (verba legis as default with absurdity-injustice escape)

stances.claim: Republic v. Manalo (April 24, 2018) illustrates plain meaning: the Filipino wife may also remarry after a valid foreign divorce, because Article 26(2) Family Code 'does not distinguish whether the Filipino spouse is the petitioner or the respondent in the foreign divorce proceeding' -- and even assuming arguendo ambiguity in 'obtained,' the Court would have construed it consistently with intent to avoid 'the absurd situation' of unequal remarriage capacity.
stances.rhetorical_move: verba-legis-plus-arguendo illustration (the Court covered both rules)

stances.claim: Under ratio legis et anima, 'a statute must be read according to its spirit or intent, for what is within the spirit is within the statute although it is not within its letter' (League of Cities v. Comelec, Dec. 21, 2009; Naval v. Comelec, July 8, 2014: 'Effect will be given the real intention even though contrary to the letter of the law').

Salvacion v. Central Bank (Aug. 21, 1997) illustrates ratio legis: the Court ignored RA 6426's letter (which exempted dollar deposits from attachment to encourage foreign-currency inflows during the 1983 'shamble' economy) and ordered the perpetrator's dollar account released to a Filipino minor rape victim's family -- because the literal application produced 'outright injustice and inequality.'
stances.rhetorical_move: ratio-legis illustration with named case and historical context

stances.claim: Civil Code Article 10 is CJ's personal lodestar -- 'In case of doubt ... it is presumed that the lawmaking body intended right and justice to prevail' -- and he decided cases as a sitting jurist 'pursuant to my firm belief, after prayer and reflection, to achieve right and justice.'
Manalo (verba legis) and Salvacion (ratio legis) are both correct because each produced right and justice -- the two methods are not in opposition, but tools that converge when applied properly.
stances.rhetorical_move: harmonization framing (both methods serve the same end)

notable_anecdotes: Pilares introduced with his credentials in one sentence ('Ateneo law valedictorian, and second placer in the 2006 bar exams') -- endorsing the book and the author simultaneously.

Republic v. Manalo: Filipino wife secured valid foreign divorce that capacitated the foreigner husband to remarry -- but the SC held she too could remarry under Article 26(2), refusing to read 'INITIATED' into the statute.

League of Cities v. Comelec quote so circumlocutorily framed that CJ challenges readers to 'reread that quote from the Court and see whether you can figure it out' -- a rare gentle critique of SC prose.

Salvacion v. Central Bank facts: Filipino minor detained and raped by an American tourist who escaped to flee the country, indefinite delay of criminal case, family files separate civil suit for damages -- the bank invoked RA 6426's attachment exemption -- Court ignored the statute's letter and released the dollar deposits 'in anguish' to the victim.

RA 6426's 1983 enactment context: 'the economy was in a shamble' and needed foreign-currency-deposit incentives -- Court conceded 'the intention of the questioned law may have been good' but 'failed to anticipate the iniquitous effects.'

Personal disclosure: 'When I was an incumbent, I leaned on Article 10 of the Civil Code ... I decided on cases pursuant to my firm belief, after prayer and reflection, to achieve right and justice' -- embedding faith into juridical practice.
Closing harmonization: both Manalo (plain meaning) and Salvacion (spirit) are correct because each produced right and justice -- the methods are tools, the standard is right-and-justice.

one_paragraph_summary: Prompted by senators and readers asking how the newly-passed Maharlika Investment Fund (MIF) law should be read -- 'according to the language used or according to the intents of the authors?' -- Panganiban opens with the concession that 'the question seems simple but there is no simple answer,' and endorses Prof. Ricardo M. Pilares III's revised 'Statutory Construction: Concept and Cases' (Ateneo law valedictorian, 2006 bar second placer) as a layman-accessible guide. The basic principle, agreed with Pilares, is to find the meaning intended by the framers and apply it via verba legis (plain meaning) or ratio legis (spirit/reason). Under verba legis, lawmakers are 'presumed to know the meaning of the words, to have used such words advisedly, and to have expressed their intent by the use of such words as are found in the statute,' with interpretation resorted to only when the literal meaning would be 'impossible, absurd or would lead to injustice' -- illustrated by Republic v. Manalo (April 24, 2018), where a Filipino wife whose foreign husband secured a valid divorce was held capacitated to remarry under Article 26(2) Family Code because the statute does not distinguish petitioner from respondent, the Court even noting arguendo that any ambiguity in 'obtained' would be construed against the 'absurd situation' of unequal remarriage. The second rule, ratio legis et anima ('the reason of the law is the soul of the law'), was illustrated in League of Cities v. Comelec (Dec. 21, 2009) -- 'what is within the spirit is within the statute although it is not within its letter' -- and Naval v. Comelec (July 8, 2014) -- 'effect will be given the real intention even though contrary to the letter of the law' -- and dramatized in Salvacion v. Central Bank (Aug. 21, 1997), where the Court ignored RA 6426's letter (which had exempted dollar deposits from attachment to incentivize foreign-currency inflows when the 1983 economy was 'in a shamble') and ordered the release of an escaped American tourist's dollar deposits to a Filipino minor rape victim's family because literal application produced 'outright injustice and inequality.' CJ closes with his own interpretive lodestar -- Civil Code Article 10, 'In case of doubt ... it is presumed that the lawmaking body intended right and justice to prevail' -- which he applied as an incumbent justice 'after prayer and reflection,' and finds both Manalo (verba legis) and Salvacion (ratio legis) correct because each produced right and justice.
